newsitem.title: UK: UK Building societies buoyed by Nationwide.
newsitem.headline: UK Building societies buoyed by Nationwide.

text.p: Britain's remaining building societies breathed a collective sigh of relief on Wednesday when the largest among them, the Nationwide, won a resounding victory in a battle against a group wanting it to shed its mutuality.

Nationwide -- which calls itself "the world's number one building society" after Britain's biggest home lender Halifax converted to bank status -- might have been forced along the same path if five pro-conversion directors had been elected.

Led by self-proclaimed "freelance butler" Michael Hardern, the challengers stood on a "conversion" ticket and offered the Nationwide's members -- its savers and borrowers -- a thousand pound ($1,680) windfall if voted onto the board. But the Nationwide's own directors were re-elected by a large margin by the 1.35 million members who voted in the ballot.

If the vote had gone against the Nationwide, industry sources predicted others such as Bradford & Bingley and Britannia would have been forced to reassess their commitment to mutuality -- where borrowers and savers actually own the society.

"This is not just a victory for the Nationwide, but a vote of confidence for the whole mutual building society sector," Adrian Coles, director-general of the Building Societies Association (BSA) said in a statement.
The building societies said the result showed they could offer better returns than many banks.
Analysts say the Nationwide could be worth more than seven billion pounds ($11.8 billion) if floated on the stock exchange, with members in line for a share pay-out of between 1,000 and 2,000 pounds.

Alternatively the Nationwide could put itself up for sale to the highest bidder, guaranteeing its members a cash payment. Earlier, former building society Alliance & Leicester denied a report it was discussing a bid for Nationwide.
Brian Davis, the Nationwide's chief executive, has repeatedly warned that ditching mutuality would give a short term benefit but people would be worse off in the long run.
Building societies have been the mainstay lenders to Britain's homeowners since the establishment of the first known society in 1775 at the Golden Cross Inn in Birmingham, central England.
The earliest societies were wound up when all their members had been housed and were known as "terminating" societies.
They were confined to the Midlands and the north of England, according to a history of the movement compiled by the Building Societies Association (BSA), the trade association for the industry.

London's first building society, the Greenwich Union, was established in 1809. A court case in 1812 ruled in the society's favour over arrears in payments to it -- the first formal recognition of building societies' rights.
By 1825, there were more than 250 societies in existence throughout the country and in 1832 the Great Reform Act resulted in a rapidly increased growth in the industry.

During the nineteenth century the movement became more sophisticated and legislation was passed to deal specifically with building societies. By the 1840s societies began to accept savings from members who were not necessarily potential home owners.
The first known permanent society was formed in 1845 and by 1860 the number of societies in London had mushroomed to more than 750, with 2,000 in the rest of the country.

In 1892 the country's largest building society, the Liberator Permanent Benefit, collapsed. This led to the 1894 Building Societies Act, which closed loopholes and guarded against a recurrence of the Liberator fiasco.
In 1910 there were 1,723 societies with 626,000 members and total assets of over 76 million pounds.
But in 1988, Abbey National became the first to say it would convert to Plc status, an option given to it under the Building Societies Act of 1986.
Abbey National converted in July 1989, but it was six years before Halifax said it would also follow the conversion path.
Woolwich, Alliance & Leicester have also become banks and Northern Rock plans to do the same, while Bristol and West merged with Bank of Ireland.
There are now only 72 societies, with millions of members around the country and tens of billions of pounds in assets. ($ = 0.595 British Pounds)
